title: Graph and Vector: Combining Relationship and Semantic Search

questions.q: What are the three production patterns for combining graph structure and vector similarity?
options: Pre-filter by graph then rank by vector; post-retrieve by vector then expand/filter by graph; graph-guided vector traversal that uses relationships to decide what context to gather
Store graphs and vectors in the same column; index everything with B-trees; shard randomly
Replace vector search with graph search entirely
Run graph queries first, then delete the vector index
questions.explain: The chapter identifies three patterns — pre-filter by graph/rank by vector, post-retrieve by vector/expand by graph, and graph-guided traversal — chosen by whether structural constraints are known before or after the semantic query.

questions.q: Why does the chapter say index-free adjacency gives graph databases their characteristic traversal performance?
options: Because graph queries run on GPUs
Because they cache all query results in memory
Because the planner follows pointers directly from node to neighbors instead of joining tables, giving O(depth × branching_factor) instead of O(n log n) for a join-based equivalent
Because they never use indexes at all
questions.explain: Index-free adjacency follows direct pointers from node to neighbor rather than performing joins, yielding O(depth × branching_factor) traversal instead of O(n log n) join-based plans.

questions.q: What does SQL Server's native graph support look like, and what is its traversal limit?
options: SQL Server has no graph support; you must use a separate database

Graph tables via CREATE TABLE AS NODE / AS EDGE since 2017 with MATCH ASCII-art arrow syntax; MATCH cannot express variable-length paths in one clause, so deep traversal uses recursive CTEs or SHORTEST_PATH (2022)
Native Cypher support since 2017 with unlimited path expressions
Graph tables that only work with the VECTOR type
questions.explain: SQL Server 2017 introduced AS NODE / AS EDGE tables with MATCH arrow syntax; unlike Cypher it cannot express variable-length paths in a single MATCH clause, hence explicit CTE hop expansion or SHORTEST_PATH from 2022.

questions.q: What is the hop penalty in the SQL Server graph-vector example, and how should it be tuned?
options: Fixed at 1.0 and never changed
Always 0.5 regardless of graph type
Hop penalties are not used in SQL Server

0.85 per hop, tunable: 0.75–0.85 for citation networks where relevance decays sharply with distance, 0.95 or none for social graphs where second-degree connections stay relevant — benchmarked against a human-labeled relevance set
questions.explain: The example uses a 0.85 per-hop penalty as a tunable parameter: sharper decay (0.75–0.85) for citation networks, near-flat (0.95 or none) for social graphs, validated against human-labeled relevance.

questions.q: When should you keep graph-vector hybrid in SQL Server versus moving to a native graph-vector engine?
options: Always use a dedicated graph database regardless of depth

At one to two hops, SQL Server with a well-indexed adjacency table performs comparably and eliminates operational complexity; beyond three hops, T-SQL recursive CTEs get slow and Neo4j or Amazon Neptune Analytics handle it naturally
SQL Server can never do graph-vector hybrid
Only when the data volume is under 100 rows
questions.explain: Relationship depth is the primary driver: 1–2 hops work fine in SQL Server, but queries needing more than three hops make recursive CTEs slow and awkward — that's when Neo4j or Neptune Analytics earn their keep.
